title: Cranial and Spinal Nerves
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the twelve cranial nerves, the brachial plexus and the major nerves of the upper and lower limbs, the dermatomes, and the brainstem circuit for horizontal gaze. Board questions almost always start from a deficit, such as a down-and-out eye, a drooping lower face, a wrist drop, a foot drop, or a numb lateral foot, and ask which nerve, root, or tract is damaged and where. The reliable way to answer is to know what each nerve supplies, where it runs, and which muscles are left unopposed when it fails, so that every sign can be reasoned out rather than memorized.

connections.how: Parasympathetic fibers ride in CN III, VII, IX, and X, and T1 sympathetic outflow explains Horner syndrome in lower plexus injuries.

terms.def: A motor neuron in a brainstem nucleus or the spinal ventral horn whose axon reaches skeletal muscle directly; its loss causes weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, and reduced reflexes.
A cortical or brainstem neuron whose axon descends to synapse on lower motor neurons; its loss causes weakness with spasticity and hyperreflexia below the lesion.
The UMN pathway from motor cortex to the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves.
Motor fibers to muscles derived from the pharyngeal arches, carried by CN V, VII, IX, and X.
The area of skin supplied by the sensory fibers of a single spinal nerve root.
The group of muscles supplied mainly by a single spinal nerve root.
The network formed by the ventral rami of C5 to T1 that supplies the upper limb.
Drop of the pelvis on the unsupported side when standing on one leg, caused by weak hip abductors on the stance side.
A paired brainstem tract that, among other connections, carries axons from the abducens nucleus on one side to the medial rectus motor neurons of the oculomotor nucleus on the other side.
The pontine gaze center that generates horizontal saccades toward its own side.
Impaired adduction of one eye on lateral gaze, with nystagmus of the opposite abducting eye, caused by a lesion of the MLF.
Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root, producing pain, sensory loss, weakness, and reflex change in that root's distribution.

sections.title: The cranial nerves: foramina, components, and deficits

blocks.text: Cranial nerves carry the fiber types of spinal nerves plus special senses and branchial motor fibers, but each carries only some of them, so each lesion produces a distinctive combination of losses. Their attachments follow a fixed order: I and II to the forebrain, III and IV to the midbrain, V to the pons, VI, VII, and VIII at the pontomedullary junction, IX, X, and XII to the medulla, and the spinal part of XI to the upper cervical cord. That order, together with the foramen each nerve uses, places a lesion in the brainstem, at the skull base, or in the periphery.

blocks.caption: A lesion at the superior orbital fissure or jugular foramen affects every nerve passing through it.

blocks.text: Eye signs follow from the muscle that is lost and the muscles left unopposed. When CN III fails, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) pull the eye down and out, the lid falls because the levator palpebrae is paralyzed, and the pupil dilates and stops reacting because the parasympathetic supply to the sphincter is lost while sympathetic dilator tone remains. Pupillary fibers run on the surface of the nerve, so external compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm or a herniating uncus dilates the pupil early. Diabetic microvascular infarction damages the core of the nerve and usually spares the pupil.

blocks.title: CN III compression by an aneurysm
steps: Aneurysm at the internal carotid and posterior communicating junction
Expanding sac presses on the adjacent CN III
Superficial parasympathetic pupillary fibers fail first
Pupil dilates and reacts poorly to light
Deeper somatic motor fibers then fail
Ptosis and a down-and-out eye follow
blocks.caption: A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil indicates compression until proven otherwise.

blocks.text: The superior oblique depresses the eye most effectively when it is adducted and also intorts it. A CN IV lesion therefore causes vertical diplopia worst when reading or descending stairs. The patient tilts the head away from the lesion, because tilting toward it demands intorsion from the weak muscle and lets the superior rectus elevate the eye further. CN IV is the only nerve to leave the dorsal brainstem, and its fibers cross first, so a trochlear nucleus lesion weakens the opposite superior oblique. CN VI supplies only the lateral rectus, leaving the eye adducted. Its long course over the clivus makes it easily stretched by raised intracranial pressure, so a sixth nerve palsy can be a false localizing sign.

Each lateral pterygoid (CN V3) pulls the jaw forward and toward the opposite side, so with one weak the jaw deviates toward the lesion on opening. Each genioglossus (CN XII) protrudes the tongue toward the opposite side, so after a CN XII lesion the intact muscle pushes the tongue toward the lesion, with atrophy and fasciculations because the LMN is lost. In the palate the intact levator veli palatini (CN X) draws the uvula away from the lesion. CN XI weakness drops the ipsilateral shoulder and weakens turning the head to the opposite side, since each sternocleidomastoid turns the face away from its own side.

blocks.title: Reflexes that test pairs of cranial nerves
blocks.caption: If one eye never blinks whichever cornea is touched, that eye's CN VII is damaged; if neither eye blinks when one cornea is touched, that side's V1 is damaged.

blocks.predict: A patient with long-standing diabetes and a patient with sudden severe headache both have ptosis and a down-and-out eye. Which one probably has a normal pupil, and why?
blocks.explain: The diabetic patient. Microvascular ischemia infarcts the center of the nerve and spares the superficial pupillary fibers, whereas an aneurysm compresses from outside and affects the pupil first.
blocks.check: The CN III paragraph and the compression flow.

blocks.text: The facial motor nucleus in the caudal pons holds the LMNs for every muscle of facial expression on its own side. The part serving the upper face (frontalis and orbicularis oculi) receives corticobulbar fibers from both hemispheres, while the part serving the lower face receives them mainly from the opposite hemisphere. This difference in UMN input, not any difference in the nerve, separates the two patterns of facial weakness.

A lesion of the motor cortex or of corticobulbar fibers in the internal capsule removes one of the two inputs to the upper face. The input from the other hemisphere keeps the forehead wrinkling and the eye closing, while the opposite lower face loses its main input, so the nasolabial fold flattens and the mouth is pulled toward the normal side. Arm weakness on the drooping side often accompanies it. Smiling in response to genuine emotion may be partly preserved, because emotional facial movement uses pathways separate from voluntary corticobulbar control.

A lesion of the facial nucleus or nerve removes the final common pathway for the entire half of the face. The forehead cannot wrinkle, the eye cannot close and rolls upward on attempted closure (Bell phenomenon), the corneal blink is lost on that side, and the mouth sags. The usual cause is Bell palsy, an acute idiopathic CN VII palsy thought to arise from viral inflammation (reactivated herpes simplex virus is suspected) with swelling of the nerve inside the narrow facial canal. Other causes include varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion (Ramsay Hunt syndrome, with vesicles in the ear), Lyme disease (sometimes bilateral), parotid tumors, temporal bone fracture, and tumors in the internal acoustic meatus. Within the pons, CN VII fibers loop around the abducens nucleus beneath the facial colliculus, so a pontine lesion there often adds an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy.

rows: May be affected, depending on site
Contralateral arm weakness, aphasia if dominant hemisphere

blocks.caption: Forehead strength is the single most useful bedside distinction.

blocks.text: Branches leave CN VII at fixed points in the temporal bone, so the accompanying findings place a peripheral lesion along its course.

blocks.title: Course of CN VII and the branches that localize a lesion
steps: Pons: motor nucleus; fibers loop around abducens nucleus

blocks.title: Placing a CN VII lesion
blocks.text: A patient cannot wrinkle the right forehead or close the right eye, and the right mouth droops. Forehead involvement makes this a CN VII lesion, not a stroke. Sounds are painfully loud in the right ear and taste is lost on the right anterior tongue, but tearing is normal. Hyperacusis means the nerve to stapedius is involved, and lost taste means the chorda tympani is involved, so the lesion lies at or above the stapedius branch. Normal tearing means the greater petrosal nerve, which leaves at the geniculate ganglion, is spared. The lesion is in the facial canal between the geniculate ganglion and the stapedius branch. A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen, such as a parotid tumor, would cause facial weakness alone.

sections.title: The brachial plexus and upper limb nerve injuries

blocks.text: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of C5 to T1. The roots join into three trunks above the clavicle, each trunk splits into an anterior and a posterior division behind the clavicle, the divisions regroup into three cords in the axilla, and the cords end in five terminal branches. Anterior divisions supply the flexor (anterior) compartments and posterior divisions supply the extensor (posterior) compartments, which is why the posterior cord gives rise to both the axillary and radial nerves. The cords are named for their position around the axillary artery.

blocks.title: Organization of the brachial plexus
rows: Dorsal scapular (C5); long thoracic (C5 to C7)
Upper C5 to C6; middle C7; lower C8 to T1
Anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) from each trunk
Anterior divisions of upper and middle trunks
blocks.caption: The median nerve receives roots from both the lateral and medial cords.

blocks.text: Forcing the head and shoulder apart, as in shoulder dystocia or a fall onto the shoulder, stretches the upper trunk (Erb palsy, C5 to C6). The deltoid and supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (lateral rotation), and biceps and brachialis (elbow flexion and supination) fail, so the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated with the elbow extended and forearm pronated (waiter's tip). Sensation is reduced over the lateral arm and forearm, and the biceps reflex is lost.

Pulling the abducted arm upward, as when grabbing a support during a fall or in a breech delivery, stretches the lower trunk (Klumpke palsy, C8 to T1). The intrinsic hand muscles fail. Because the lumbricals and interossei normally flex the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extend the interphalangeal (IP) joints, their loss lets the long extensors hyperextend the MCPs and the long flexors flex the IPs, producing a claw hand, with sensory loss along the medial forearm and hand. Avulsion of the T1 root also interrupts preganglionic sympathetic fibers bound for the head, adding ipsilateral Horner syndrome (mild ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). A cervical rib or an apical lung (Pancoast) tumor compresses the same trunk gradually.

blocks.caption: Each nerve is injured where it lies on bone or passes through a tunnel.

blocks.text: The radial nerve gives its branches to the triceps before it enters the radial groove, so a midshaft fracture spares elbow extension but paralyzes the wrist and finger extensors. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so carpal tunnel syndrome numbs the fingers but spares the skin over the thenar eminence. The serratus anterior holds the scapula against the chest wall and rotates it upward, so its loss lets the medial border lift away when the patient pushes against a wall and limits elevation of the arm.

blocks.predict: Why is clawing of the ring and little fingers more obvious after an ulnar lesion at the wrist than after one at the elbow?
blocks.explain: An elbow lesion also paralyzes the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, so the distal IP joints of digits 4 and 5 are not pulled into flexion. A wrist lesion spares that muscle, so the unopposed long flexor bends the fingers more and the claw is more marked.
blocks.check: The Klumpke paragraph on what the lumbricals and interossei do, and the ulnar row of the nerve injury table.

blocks.text: Lower limb nerves are injured where they cross bone or pass close to surgical and injection sites, and each deficit follows from the muscle compartment the nerve supplies. The sciatic nerve divides above the knee into the tibial nerve, which supplies the posterior compartment of the leg and the sole, and the common fibular (peroneal) nerve, which supplies the anterior and lateral compartments.

The common fibular nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, where a fracture, a tight cast, a knee brace, or prolonged leg crossing compresses it. Its deep branch supplies the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior and the toe extensors, which dorsiflex the foot and toes) and the skin of the first web space. Its superficial branch supplies the lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis, which evert the foot) and most of the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg. Injury causes foot drop: the toes catch during swing, so the patient lifts the knee high (steppage gait) and the foot slaps at heel strike. Inversion is largely preserved because tibialis posterior, the main invertor, is supplied by the tibial nerve.

The tibial nerve supplies gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior, and the long toe flexors. A proximal injury, as in posterior knee dislocation, severely weakens plantar flexion and inversion, so the patient cannot stand on the toes, the Achilles reflex falls, and the sole is numb. Compression in the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus affects only the plantar nerves, numbing the sole and weakening the intrinsic foot muscles.

The femoral nerve (L2 to L4) passes under the inguinal ligament to the quadriceps. Its loss makes the knee buckle, especially on stairs, reduces the patellar reflex, and numbs the anterior thigh and, through the saphenous branch, the medial leg. The obturator nerve (L2 to L4) runs along the lateral pelvic wall to the thigh adductors and can be compressed during pelvic surgery, pelvic fracture, or a difficult labor, causing weak adduction and a numb patch on the medial thigh.

The superior gluteal nerve (L4 to S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae, which abduct the hip and, during single-leg stance, hold the pelvis level against body weight. It is injured by a poorly placed gluteal injection or hip surgery. The sign appears on the opposite side from the lesion, as the flow shows.

sections.title: Dermatomes and localizing a nerve root lesion

blocks.text: Each spinal nerve root carries sensory fibers whose cell bodies lie in one dorsal root ganglion, and the strip of skin those fibers supply is its dermatome. Dermatomes reflect segmental development of the embryo: the limbs grow out carrying their segments with them, so dermatomes run as bands around the trunk but as long strips down the limbs. A root lesion produces sensory change in a dermatome, weakness in a myotome, and loss of the reflex served by that root, whereas a peripheral nerve lesion stays within that nerve's own sensory field and muscles.

blocks.title: Root landmarks for localization
rows: Lateral leg and dorsum of foot, great toe
Great toe extension, foot inversion, hip abduction
Lateral foot and little toe, sole
Anal and urethral sphincters (S2 to S4)
blocks.caption: Matching dermatome, myotome, and reflex together localizes a root best.

blocks.text: Adjacent dermatomes overlap, especially for light touch, so a single root lesion usually produces reduced rather than absent sensation and is best detected with pinprick. For spinal cord lesions, a sensory level at the nipple places a cord lesion at or above T4, and one at the umbilicus at or above T10, because ascending tracts carry everything from below.

Root numbering explains which root a herniated disc compresses. In the cervical spine each root exits above the vertebra of the same number (C8 exits between C7 and T1), so a C5 to C6 disc compresses the C6 root and numbs the thumb. In the lumbar spine each root exits below its pedicle, high in its foramen, above the disc. The usual posterolateral herniation therefore misses the root exiting at that level and compresses the root descending to the next foramen.

blocks.title: L4 to L5 disc herniation
steps: Annulus fibrosus tears posterolaterally, beside the posterior longitudinal ligament
Nucleus pulposus herniates at the L4 to L5 disc
Descending L5 root is compressed in the lateral recess
Pain radiates down the lateral leg to the dorsum of the foot
Weak great toe extension and dorsiflexion; no reflex lost
blocks.caption: An L5 to S1 herniation compresses S1 instead, numbing the lateral foot and reducing the Achilles reflex.

blocks.text: Varicella zoster virus lies latent in a dorsal root ganglion, so its reactivation (shingles) produces a painful vesicular band confined to one dermatome. Visceral pain is referred to the dermatome sharing the visceral afferents' spinal segment: early appendicitis is felt at the umbilicus (T10), and diaphragmatic irritation is felt at the shoulder because the phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5.

blocks.title: Root or nerve? Two patients with foot drop
blocks.text: Patient A has foot drop, weak eversion, normal inversion, normal hip abduction, and numbness on the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg. Patient B has foot drop, weak inversion and hip abduction, and numbness of the dorsum of the foot with back pain radiating down the leg. Both lack dorsiflexion (deep fibular nerve, L4 and L5). Inversion (tibialis posterior) is supplied by the tibial nerve and hip abduction (gluteus medius) by the superior gluteal nerve, yet both draw on L5. Weakness across three nerves sharing one root places Patient B's lesion at the L5 root, most likely an L4 to L5 disc. Patient A's deficit stays within the common fibular nerve, consistent with compression at the fibular neck.

Looking to one side requires the lateral rectus of one eye (CN VI) and the medial rectus of the other (CN III) to contract together, although their nuclei lie in different parts of the brainstem. The abducens nucleus coordinates them. It contains motor neurons for the ipsilateral lateral rectus and also internuclear neurons whose axons cross the midline and ascend in the opposite medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the medial rectus motor neurons of the oculomotor nucleus.

blocks.title: Circuit for horizontal gaze to the right
steps: Left frontal eye field signals a rightward saccade
Right PPRF generates the horizontal saccade command
Right abducens nucleus: motor neurons fire to the right lateral rectus
Right abducens internuclear axons cross to the left MLF
Left MLF ascends to the left oculomotor medial rectus neurons
Left medial rectus contracts; both eyes turn right
blocks.caption: Each abducens nucleus is a gaze center for its own side, not just the nucleus of one muscle.

blocks.text: A lesion of the MLF cuts this link on one side. On gaze away from the lesion, the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct or adducts slowly, while the opposite, abducting eye overshoots with horizontal nystagmus. The leading explanation is that the brain increases the command to overcome the weak adduction, and because yoked muscles receive equal innervation, the abducting eye receives the excess too. The syndrome is named for the side of the lesion, which is the side of the eye that fails to adduct.

Convergence is preserved because it uses a separate midbrain vergence pathway that reaches the medial rectus neurons directly, without the MLF. An eye that cannot adduct on lateral gaze but adducts normally during convergence therefore has an intact medial rectus, CN III, and oculomotor nucleus, which proves the lesion is internuclear. The abducting eye is normal, distinguishing INO from a CN VI palsy, and there is no ptosis or pupil change, distinguishing it from a CN III palsy.

The MLF is a compact, heavily myelinated tract near the floor of the fourth ventricle, where multiple sclerosis (MS) plaques commonly form. Demyelination slows or blocks conduction in the internuclear axons, so mild cases show only slowed adduction during saccades. Bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests MS. A unilateral INO in an older adult more often reflects a small brainstem infarct in paramedian branches of the basilar artery. If a lesion damages the PPRF or abducens nucleus together with the adjacent MLF on the same side, the result is the one-and-a-half syndrome: no horizontal gaze toward the lesion and, on gaze away, no adduction of the eye on the lesion side, leaving abduction of the opposite eye as the only horizontal movement.

rows: Right eye fails to adduct; left eye abducts with nystagmus
Right PPRF or abducens nucleus plus right MLF
Only the left eye abducts, with nystagmus
Right eye fails to adduct, no nystagmus
Right eye fails to adduct; ptosis and dilated pupil
blocks.caption: Convergence and the other cranial nerve signs separate an MLF lesion from a CN III or CN VI palsy.

blocks.predict: A 28-year-old cannot adduct either eye on lateral gaze, each abducting eye shows nystagmus, and both eyes converge normally. Where is the lesion and what disease is most likely?
blocks.explain: Both MLFs are damaged (bilateral INO). Normal convergence shows that both medial recti and oculomotor nuclei work, so the defect is in the internuclear pathway, and bilateral involvement in a young adult points to MS.
blocks.check: The convergence paragraph and the MS paragraph.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology predict where nerves are injured. Cranial nerves crowd through shared foramina, so a skull base lesion at the superior orbital fissure or jugular foramen takes out a group, while a brainstem lesion combines a cranial nerve deficit on one side with long tract signs on the other. Limb nerves fail where they press against bone or pass through tunnels, and segmental development of the embryo explains why roots map to dermatomes and myotomes that cross several peripheral nerve territories. That overlap is how root lesions are told apart from nerve lesions.

Pathology, microbiology, and immunology supply the causes. Aneurysms and microvascular ischemia separate pupil-involving from pupil-sparing third nerve palsies, herpes viruses and Borrelia burgdorferi cause facial palsy, varicella zoster reactivates in a single dorsal root ganglion, and immune-mediated demyelination in MS targets the MLF. Bedside localization has limits: dermatome maps differ among sources, single roots overlap, and anomalous innervation is common in the hand, so a pattern that does not fit should prompt a search for more than one lesion.

summary: Each cranial nerve has a fixed brainstem level and skull exit; III, IV, V1, and VI share the superior orbital fissure, and IX, X, and XI share the jugular foramen.
CN III palsy gives a down-and-out eye with ptosis; compression dilates the pupil early, while diabetic ischemia usually spares it.
The jaw (V3) and tongue (XII) deviate toward the lesion; the uvula deviates away from a CN X lesion.
The upper face receives bilateral cortical input, so a UMN lesion spares the forehead and weakens only the contralateral lower face; a CN VII lesion weakens the entire ipsilateral face.
Taste, tearing, and hyperacusis localize a CN VII lesion along its course through the temporal bone.
Erb palsy (C5 to C6) gives the waiter's tip; Klumpke palsy (C8 to T1) gives a claw hand, sometimes with Horner syndrome.
Distal nerves fail at bony sites: axillary at the surgical neck, radial at the midshaft, ulnar at the medial epicondyle, common fibular at the fibular neck.
Superior gluteal nerve injury lets the pelvis drop on the opposite, unsupported side (Trendelenburg sign).
C6 thumb, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 knee and medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot; a posterolateral L4 to L5 disc compresses the L5 root.
An MLF lesion impairs adduction of the ipsilateral eye on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye and spares convergence; bilateral INO suggests MS.

verify: Dermatome maps differ between sources (for example T4 versus T5 at the nipple and whether the medial malleolus and great toe belong to L4 or L5); landmarks follow the course competency list.
Reflex root assignments vary slightly between texts (patellar L3 to L4 or L2 to L4; triceps C7 or C7 to C8); confirm the values NABNE expects.

The classic teaching that the upper facial nucleus receives bilateral cortical input and the lower facial nucleus mainly contralateral input is a simplification of more complex cortical representation; it remains the expected exam rule.
The association of Bell palsy with herpes simplex virus reactivation is supported but not proven; it is stated as suspected.
The explanation of abducting nystagmus in INO (increased yoked innervation) is one of several proposed mechanisms.
The functional classification of CN XI (branchial versus somatic motor) varies between texts and is given here simply as motor.
Root contributions of individual nerves (for example median C5 to T1 versus C6 to T1, common fibular L4 to S2) vary slightly among anatomical texts.
Confirm whether NABNE uses fibular or peroneal, and whether eponyms such as Erb, Klumpke, Guyon, Ramsay Hunt, and Bell phenomenon are expected.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: brachial-plexus (roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches), dermatome-map (front and back), cn-brainstem (cranial nerve attachments and skull foramina), and mlf-gaze (horizontal gaze circuit with MLF lesion sites).
